title: Esau runs
hookLine: twenty years after being cheated, Esau runs to embrace Jacob (Genesis 33:4)

cards: Dust on the horizon. Jacob looks up, and there is his brother Esau with, the text says, four hundred men.
The last time they were together, Jacob dressed up as Esau, fooled their blind father, and walked off with the blessing meant for his brother. Esau said in his heart that he would kill him.
Jacob ran, and stayed away a long time; in his own words to his father-in-law, twenty years. Now he's coming home, limping from a night of wrestling by the river.
He has sent gifts ahead, wave after wave, and split his camp in two in case one half is attacked. And now he walks out in front of them all.

teach.b: First, Jacob bows. The King James says he "bowed himself to the ground seven times, until he came near to his brother." It's the posture of a man expecting the worst.
Here is the whole surprise, in one verse: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." No speech first. No terms.
No demand for an apology. The text never says what changed in Esau. It only shows us his feet.

Jacob keeps pressing the flocks on him, and Esau waves them off: "I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself." Jacob insists: "Take, I pray thee, my blessing that is brought to thee."
Some readers notice the word. Blessing. The very thing he stole, and now he's trying to hand a blessing back.

teach.h: AS THOUGH THE FACE OF GOD.
teach.b: Jacob says: "I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God." The night before, he had wrestled until dawn and named the place for seeing God face to face. Now he says it of his brother.
Readers have heard different things in that line. One reading: a face that should have been angry and is kind instead is about as close to the divine as it gets. The story doesn't tie a bow on it.
The brothers soon part ways again. But for one morning, the wronged one ran.

how: Jews read the meeting of Jacob and Esau in the yearly cycle of Torah readings in synagogue, and Christians read it in Genesis; it is taught as a story of brothers reconciled after a deep wrong.

games.q: you're Esau. the brother who cheated you of your blessing is bowing to the ground ahead of you, again and again. what do you do?
o: make him finish bowing, then hear him out.
run to meet him and embrace him.
turn your men around and leave.
games.why: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." the wronged one moves first.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've drifted from, where things went quiet after a hurt on either side, and ask only: what is one step toward them?

A message that just says hello, a photo, a question about their kids: choose the smallest step that's still a step, and let your feet feel the floor. If you pray, you can hold this person in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Esau runs. Years after Jacob cheated him of the blessing, Esau runs to meet his brother, embraces him, and they weep. Today's word.
